explanations.explanation: Dead, friend. Paul says it flat out: "And you were dead in your trespasses and sins," (Ephesians 2:1). Not struggling, not limping along. Dead. That's why what comes next hits so hard.

I get why "weak" sounds right, since it's gentler. But Paul doesn't soften it. He says "you were dead in your trespasses and sins," (Ephesians 2:1). A weak person can still lift a finger, and Paul is describing something much bigger than that.

"Sick" feels close, like you just need some soup and a nap. Paul uses a bigger word: "you were dead in your trespasses and sins," (Ephesians 2:1). A sick person is still waiting to get better, and Paul says dead. I think that makes the good news even louder.

I see why you'd lean that way, but Paul says the opposite. He calls it "the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:2). That word "now" is doing the heavy lifting. The text says it's at work, not finished.
That's right, friend. Paul describes "the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:2). Now, as in still going. He doesn't say it packed up and left, so neither do I.

explanations.answer: All of us with Paul included
explanations.explanation: Yes, and notice Paul doesn't point a finger from a distance. He writes, "All of us also lived among them at one time," (Ephesians 2:3). He puts himself right in the group. I like a teacher who says "us" and not "you people."

Close, but Paul leaves himself in the picture. He says, "All of us also lived among them at one time," (Ephesians 2:3). That "us" covers him too. He's not lecturing from the balcony, he's standing in the same room.

The sons of disobedience come up right before this, so I see the mix-up. But Paul says, "All of us also lived among them at one time," (Ephesians 2:3). "Among them" means he and his readers were in that crowd too. Nobody gets to sit this one out.
True. Paul writes, "Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath." (Ephesians 2:3). Heavy line, I know. That's the "before," and Paul is about to flip the whole page.

This one is heavy, so I understand wanting to push back. But Paul does say it: "Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath." (Ephesians 2:3). He includes himself with "we." The good news is that Paul doesn't stop there, and the next verse starts with "But."

That's it, baker. Paul says, "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy," (Ephesians 2:4). The reason is His love, plain and simple. We brought nothing to the table but crumbs, and He showed up anyway.

explanations.answer: Because we earned a second chance
explanations.explanation: I wish I could say I earned mine, but Paul gives a different reason. He says, "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy," (Ephesians 2:4). A dead person can't earn anything. It was His love that moved Him.

explanations.answer: Because we finally called out to Him
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, but that's not the reason Paul gives. He says, "But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy," (Ephesians 2:4). The text names His love, and doesn't say we called out first. Dead folks don't make many phone calls, if you know what I mean.

explanations.answer: Even when they were dead in their trespasses
explanations.explanation: Right on time, and by time I mean the worst possible time. Paul says God "made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses." (Ephesians 2:5). He didn't wait for them to clean up first. That's some kind of timing.

explanations.answer: Once they stopped walking in their sins
explanations.explanation: I get it, we usually figure we have to tidy up before company comes. But Paul says God "made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses." (Ephesians 2:5). The word is "even when," not "once they stopped." God didn't wait for the house to be clean.

explanations.answer: After their prayers had been heard
explanations.explanation: That sounds reasonable, but Paul doesn't mention prayers here. He says God "made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses." (Ephesians 2:5). The timing is "even when," right in the middle of the dead part.
Grace! Paul says, "It is by grace you have been saved!" (Ephesians 2:5). Look at that exclamation point, he couldn't hold it in. I'd hop right off my gold base too, and I would still land on it.
I see why "law" came to mind, it's a big word in the Bible. But Paul says, "It is by grace you have been saved!" (Ephesians 2:5). Grace is the answer, and he even added an exclamation point to it.

Wisdom is a good thing, but it's not what Paul shouts about here. He says, "It is by grace you have been saved!" (Ephesians 2:5). Grace is the word, and it comes with an exclamation point. Paul was clearly excited.

Seated, baker! Paul says God "raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus," (Ephesians 2:6). Raised up and seated, both with Christ. It's a seat at the table, not a spot by the door.

"Crowned" has a nice ring to it, I'll give you that. But Paul's word is "seated." He says God "raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus," (Ephesians 2:6). Sitting with Christ is the picture Paul paints.

Hid? Friend, that's the opposite of what Paul says. He says God "raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus," (Ephesians 2:6). Nobody's tucked away in a corner here. They're seated with Christ.

explanations.answer: To display the riches of His grace
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul says it was "in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace," (Ephesians 2:7). The purpose is to show off His grace. It's His kindness on display, not ours.

explanations.answer: To display the strength of His people
explanations.explanation: That's a flattering thought, but Paul points somewhere else. He says it was "in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace," (Ephesians 2:7). The spotlight is on His grace, not on our muscles. I'm happy to stay out of the spotlight, I'm mostly mustache anyway.

explanations.answer: To display His anger at the world
explanations.explanation: After verse 3 I can see why you'd think that. But look where Paul lands: "in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace," (Ephesians 2:7). The display is grace, shown in kindness to us in Christ Jesus. That's the whole point.

A gift! Paul says, "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God," (Ephesians 2:8). Not from ourselves, so we didn't make it and we didn't earn it. You just open it.

A reward would mean we earned it, and Paul says otherwise. He writes, "this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God," (Ephesians 2:8). Rewards get handed out for a job well done. A gift just gets handed over.

Payment is what you get when you clock in, and Paul says this isn't that. He writes, "this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God," (Ephesians 2:8). If it were wages, we'd have earned it. Instead it's a gift, and you can't invoice a gift.

True, baker. Paul says salvation is "not by works, so that no one can boast." (Ephesians 2:9). If we could earn it, we'd have something to brag about. Since it's a gift, the bragging rights go to the Giver.
I can see why you'd doubt it, but Paul does say it. The line is "not by works, so that no one can boast." (Ephesians 2:9). The reason he gives is right there in the verse: no one can boast.
Yes! Paul says, "For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works," (Ephesians 2:10). Good works are what we're created for, not how we get saved. Order matters here, friend.

Singing sounds lovely, but it's not the word Paul uses here. He says we're "created in Christ Jesus to do good works," (Ephesians 2:10). Good works are the answer in this verse. Save the singing for the shower, where I do my best work.

Good guess, since it sounds like a natural fit. But Paul's words are "created in Christ Jesus to do good works," (Ephesians 2:10). He doesn't mention commandments in this verse. The text says good works, so I'll stick with that.

I get why you'd think so, but Paul says it the other way around. The good works are ones "which God prepared in advance as our way of life." (Ephesians 2:10). God did the planning ahead of time. We don't have to come up with the list ourselves.

Right, baker. Paul says the good works are ones "which God prepared in advance as our way of life." (Ephesians 2:10). God prepared them in advance, so the planning isn't on our shoulders. That's a relief, because my planning is mostly "more chocolate chips."
